patient.name: Tomasz Nowak
patient.complaint: Sudden severe left loin pain coming in waves since 4am
background: Warehouse supervisor in Croydon; works long hot shifts
Drinks little water; high-protein gym diet

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with colicky loin-to-groin pain and blood on dipstick, or 'most likely stone type' from the organism, urine pH or X-ray appearance.

points: Tomasz, 38, woke at 4am with **left loin pain**.
Comes in **waves**, shooting down to his left groin.
Pacing the cubicle, cannot lie still; vomited twice.
Works in a hot warehouse; drinks little water.

visual.title: Where Tomasz's pain is
visual.caption: Loin pain radiating towards the groin: the path of the ureter.

steps.text: Colicky pain that follows the ureter from loin to groin is renal colic until proven otherwise.

steps.lead: Tomasz has the full picture: **colicky loin-to-groin pain**, vomiting, tachycardia and restlessness. Check his temperature: fever is the red flag.
Tomasz most likely has a **calcium oxalate** stone, the commonest type.
Hot warehouse, little water and a high-protein gym diet: Tomasz is **dehydrated** and protein-loaded.

steps.q: Tomasz is writhing and cannot get comfortable. How does this help you?
steps.r: Colic makes patients **move around**; peritonitis makes them lie very still.

steps.lead: Tomasz's story is the classic ureteric stone. A **staghorn** stone would point to Proteus and alkaline urine.
Stone type decides what you see on imaging and how you prevent the next one.
If Tomasz becomes **febrile**, his stone may be blocking an infected kidney: an emergency.

steps.text: Fever with a stone is not 'just colic'. Infection behind an obstruction needs **urgent decompression**.

investigation.exam: Expect gold standard (non-contrast CT KUB), ultrasound in pregnancy and a pregnancy test in women of childbearing age.

steps.q: Which test should Tomasz have first, at the bedside?
steps.r: A dipstick looks for **blood** (and infection) in minutes. CT confirms afterwards.

steps.title: Tomasz's first results
steps.text: Blood without infection, normal kidney function: classic uncomplicated renal colic.

steps.lead: Tomasz had his dipstick and U&Es. In a woman of childbearing age, add a **pregnancy test** to exclude ectopic.

points: **7 mm** stone in the left mid ureter.

steps.lead: Tomasz's **CT KUB** is the gold standard and shows the stone, its size and the hydronephrosis.

visual.title: Stone size decides the treatment
visual.label: Tomasz 7 mm
visual.caption: Tomasz's 7 mm stone is suitable for medical expulsive therapy with tamsulosin.

steps.lead: If Tomasz were a **pregnant** woman, ultrasound would replace CT.

steps.text: Do not send a pregnant woman for CT KUB. **Ultrasound** first.

management.exam: Expect analgesia (IM diclofenac), size-based treatment (<5 mm, <10 mm, <2 cm, >2 cm) and the infected obstructed kidney (nephrostomy plus IV antibiotics).

steps.q: Tomasz is in severe pain. Which analgesia first?
steps.r: An **NSAID** is first-line for renal colic; IV paracetamol if NSAIDs are contraindicated.

steps.lead: Tomasz gets **IM diclofenac**. A small asymptomatic stone under 5 mm could simply be watched.
Tomasz's 7 mm stone is under 10 mm, so he starts **tamsulosin** to help it pass.

points: Left loin very tender; pain constant now.

o: Urgent percutaneous nephrostomy plus IV antibiotics
steps.r: An **infected, obstructed kidney** needs drainage now; antibiotics alone cannot reach pus behind a blockage.

steps.lead: Tomasz has an **infected obstructed kidney** with AKI: nephrostomy plus IV antibiotics. A non-infected obstruction could have a JJ stent.

visual.title: After Tomasz's nephrostomy
visual.caption: Drainage plus antibiotics: fever settles and CRP falls within days.

steps.lead: Once Tomasz is well, the stone (under 2 cm) is removed by **ureteroscopy**. Over 2 cm or staghorn would need PCNL.

steps.title: Stone management ladder
nodes: <5 mm, no symptoms: watch, image at 4 weeks

points: Advised to drink 2.5 to 3 L of water a day.

steps.lead: Tomasz has recurrent risk and hypercalciuria, so a **thiazide** is started to stop the next stone.

science.exam: Expect applied mechanisms: urease and struvite, acidic urine and uric acid, why pain radiates to the groin, how thiazides work.

steps.lead: Tomasz's concentrated urine is **supersaturated** with calcium oxalate, so crystals nucleate and grow.

steps.title: How a calcium stone forms
nodes: Stone moves into the ureter: colic

steps.lead: Tomasz's pain comes in waves because the **ureter contracts** against the stone; T11 to L2 refers it to the groin.
Tomasz's fever behind a blocked kidney is why he needed drainage, not just antibiotics.

steps.q: A patient has a staghorn calculus and urine pH 8. Which enzyme explains it?
steps.r: **Urease** from Proteus splits urea into ammonia, making urine alkaline so struvite precipitates.

steps.lead: Struvite needs **alkaline urine**, made by urease-producing bacteria such as Proteus mirabilis.
Uric acid is the opposite: it forms in **acidic urine** with high purine turnover.

visual.title: Urine pH and stone type
visual.label: Tomasz 5.8
visual.caption: Below 5.5 favours uric acid stones; alkaline urine favours struvite.

steps.lead: Tomasz's thiazide works in the **distal convoluted tubule**, reabsorbing calcium so less reaches the urine.

mcq.q: Most common composition of urinary tract stones?
mcq.r: Then uric acid and other types.

mcq.q: Which stone type is radiolucent and forms in urine pH <5.5?
mcq.r: Linked to gout, malignancy and chemotherapy.

mcq.q: Which is a red flag in suspected renal colic?
Gold-standard investigation for suspected renal colic?
Which imaging is used for renal colic in pregnancy?

mcq.r: An NSAID; IV paracetamol if contraindicated.

mcq.q: Stone over 2 cm or staghorn calculus: definitive treatment?
How do thiazides prevent calcium stone recurrence?
o: Increase calcium reabsorption in the DCT

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the pattern and the red flag.

points.p: Fever is a red flag for infection

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: concentrated urine and stone-forming salts.

prompts.q: Name the stone types, their X-ray appearance and one clue each.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: radiolucent ones are the trick.

points.p: Calcium oxalate: commonest, radiopaque, vitamin C
Uric acid: radiolucent, acidic urine pH <5.5, gout/chemo

points.p: Infected obstructed kidney: fever, flank pain, sepsis

prompts.q: What is a staghorn calculus and what causes it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: organism plus urine pH.

points.p: Struvite stone filling the renal pelvis and calyces

prompts.q: What are the first-line and gold-standard investigations for renal colic?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: initial vs diagnostic, and pregnancy.

points.p: Pregnancy test in women of childbearing age
Bloods: U&Es (and blood cultures if febrile)

prompts.q: How is a stone managed by size?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: learn the four cut-offs.

points.p: <5 mm asymptomatic: watch, image at 4 weeks

prompts.q: What is the emergency management of an obstructed kidney, and how do you prevent recurrence?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: infected or not changes the drain.

points.p: Infected obstructed kidney: urgent percutaneous nephrostomy + IV antibiotics
Obstruction with hydronephrosis/renal failure: cystoscopy and JJ stent

prompts.q: Why do struvite, uric acid and calcium stones form?

points.p: Calcium: supersaturated urine, nucleation and aggregation
Struvite: urease splits urea into ammonia, alkaline urine
Uric acid: acidic urine, high purine turnover

prompts.q: Why does the pain radiate to the groin, and how do thiazides help?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: dermatomes and the DCT.

points.p: Peristaltic ureteric contraction against the stone
Thiazides increase calcium reabsorption in the DCT

glossary.Renal colic: Severe waves of loin pain caused by a stone in the ureter.
glossary.Ureteric: Relating to the ureter, the tube from kidney to bladder.
glossary.Colicky: Pain that comes and goes in waves.
glossary.Loin: The side of the back between the ribs and the hip.
glossary.Costovertebral angle: Angle between the 12th rib and the spine, over the kidney.
glossary.Haematuria: Blood in the urine, visible or microscopic.
glossary.Hydronephrosis: Swelling of the kidney from urine backing up behind an obstruction.
glossary.Staghorn calculus: Large branching stone filling the renal pelvis and calyces, usually struvite.
glossary.Struvite: Magnesium ammonium phosphate stone formed in alkaline urine with urease-producing bacteria.
glossary.Cystine: Amino acid forming stones in a genetic condition (cystinuria).
glossary.Xanthine: Purine breakdown product that can form radiolucent stones.
glossary.Proteus mirabilis: Urease-producing Gram-negative bacterium that causes struvite stones.
glossary.Urease: Bacterial enzyme that splits urea into ammonia, making urine alkaline.
glossary.Supersaturated: Holding more dissolved salt than it can keep in solution, so crystals form.
glossary.Nucleation: The first step of crystal formation.
glossary.Periureteric fat stranding: Hazy fat around the ureter on CT, showing recent stone passage or inflammation.
glossary.CT KUB: Non-contrast CT of kidneys, ureters and bladder; gold standard for stones.
glossary.Ectopic: Pregnancy implanted outside the uterus; must be excluded in women with loin pain.
glossary.Diclofenac: An NSAID given IM as first-line analgesia for renal colic.
glossary.Tamsulosin: Alpha-blocker that relaxes ureteric smooth muscle to help stones pass.
glossary.Medical expulsive therapy: Drugs, such as tamsulosin, used to help a stone pass on its own.
glossary.ESWL: Extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy: shock waves from outside the body break up the stone.
glossary.Ureteroscopy: Camera passed up the ureter to remove or fragment a stone.
glossary.PCNL: Percutaneous nephrolithotomy: keyhole removal of a large stone through the back into the kidney.
glossary.Nephrostomy: Tube placed through the skin into the kidney to drain urine.
glossary.JJ stent: Tube from kidney to bladder placed via cystoscopy to bypass an obstruction.
glossary.Cystoscopy: Camera examination of the bladder through the urethra.
glossary.Thiazide: Diuretic that reduces urinary calcium; used to prevent calcium stones.
glossary.Hypercalciuria: Too much calcium in the urine.
glossary.Potassium citrate: Urine alkaliniser used to prevent calcium stones.
glossary.Penicillamine: Drug that binds cystine to prevent cystine stones.
glossary.Indinavir: HIV protease inhibitor linked to radiolucent stones.
glossary.DCT: Distal convoluted tubule of the nephron.
glossary.Sepsis: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by the body's response to infection.

technique.stem: A 41 year old man has had severe intermittent right loin pain since this morning. The pain comes in waves and radiates to his right groin. He has vomited twice and cannot keep still. His temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 146/88 mmHg. His abdomen is soft. Urine dipstick shows blood 2+ and is negative for nitrites and leucocytes.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis with acute flank pain: place the pain and check the dipstick.
Colicky loin-to-groin pain, restless, haematuria, no infection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A stone in the ureter: **renal colic**.

elim: Pain settles in the RIF with peritonism; this abdomen is soft.
No fever and no nitrites or leucocytes.
RUQ pain after fatty food, not loin to groin.
Older patient, shocked, pulsatile mass; he is hypertensive and young.

steps.x: **E. Ureteric calculus.** Loin to groin + restless + blood on dipstick = ureteric stone.

technique.stem: A 35 year old man has severe colicky left loin pain radiating to the groin. Urine dipstick shows blood 3+. His pain settles after IM diclofenac. His pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 138/84 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

steps.x: 'Diagnostic' = gold standard.
Classic renal colic in a non-pregnant adult.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Non-contrast CT KUB**.

elim: Misses many stones; not the gold standard.
Not first choice; less available and less sensitive for stones.
Used in pregnancy; less sensitive than CT.

steps.x: **D. Non-contrast CT KUB.** Renal colic gold standard = non-contrast CT KUB; ultrasound in pregnancy.

technique.stem: A 52 year old woman has recurrent right loin pain and urinary infections. CT KUB shows a 3 cm branching staghorn calculus in the right renal pelvis. She is now apyrexial with normal renal function.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?

steps.x: 'Definitive' for a stone of a given size: use the size thresholds.

clues: recurrent right loin pain and urinary infections
steps.x: Staghorn, over 2 cm, not infected right now.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **PCNL**.

elim: Helps stones under 10 mm pass; this cannot pass.
For ureteric or smaller stones under 2 cm.
Only for small asymptomatic stones under 5 mm.

steps.x: **B. Percutaneous nephrolithotomy.** >2 cm or staghorn = PCNL; <2 cm = ESWL or ureteroscopy.

technique.stem: A 60 year old man has recurrent calcium oxalate stones. A 24 hour urine collection shows hypercalciuria. He is started on bendroflumethiazide.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism by which this drug prevents further stones?
o: Binding of oxalate in the gut
Increased calcium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule

steps.x: Science: drug mechanism in stone prevention.
A thiazide for hypercalciuric calcium stones.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Thiazides increase **DCT calcium reabsorption**, lowering urinary calcium.
**C. Increased calcium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule.** Thiazides: less calcium in the urine.

practice.stem: A 29 year old man has had severe intermittent left flank pain radiating to the groin since last night. He is restless and has vomited. His temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 110 bpm and BP 150/92 mmHg. His abdomen is soft with left costovertebral angle tenderness.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Intermittent loin-to-groin pain with restlessness and microscopic haematuria is renal colic. Pyelonephritis needs fever and infected urine.

steps.x: Diagnosis of acute flank pain.

clues: intermittent left flank pain radiating to the groin
steps.x: Loin to groin, colicky, restless, haematuria, no infection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Renal colic** from a ureteric stone.

elim: Unlikely at 29; he is not shocked and has no pulsatile mass.
Constant LIF pain with fever in older patients.
Testicular pain and swelling; urine has blood here.

steps.x: **D. Renal colic.** Loin-to-groin colic with haematuria = renal colic.

practice.stem: A 58 year old woman has recurrent urinary tract infections and dull right loin pain. Urine culture grows Proteus mirabilis. Her urine pH is 8.0. Imaging shows a large branching calculus filling the right renal pelvis and calyces.
practice.q: Which is the most likely composition of the stone?
practice.e: Urease-producing Proteus mirabilis makes urine alkaline and precipitates struvite, forming staghorn calculi. Uric acid needs acidic urine.

steps.x: Stone composition: use the organism and pH.
Proteus + alkaline urine + staghorn.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Struvite** (triple phosphate).

elim: Commonest overall, but not linked to Proteus or alkaline urine.
Forms in acidic urine, not pH 8.
Rare; linked to indinavir in the notes, not infection.

steps.x: **C. Struvite.** Staghorn + Proteus + alkaline urine = struvite.

practice.stem: A 63 year old man with gout has right renal colic. He finished chemotherapy for lymphoma last month. A plain abdominal X-ray shows no opacity, but ultrasound shows a stone in the right renal pelvis. His pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 140/86 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely composition of the stone?
practice.e: Uric acid stones are radiolucent and form in acidic urine with high purine turnover from gout and chemotherapy. Calcium stones are radiopaque.

steps.x: Stone composition: radiolucent plus background.
Gout and cell lysis from chemotherapy, radiolucent stone, acidic urine.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Uric acid** stone.
**E. Uric acid.** Radiolucent + gout/chemotherapy + acidic urine = uric acid.

practice.stem: A 22 year old man has his third episode of renal colic. His father and sister also have recurrent kidney stones. CT shows bilateral stones with a ground-glass appearance. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely type of stone?
practice.e: Cystine stones have a genetic predisposition and a ground-glass appearance. Struvite needs infection with urease-producing bacteria.

steps.x: Stone type from the history and imaging.
Young, recurrent, familial, ground-glass.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Cystine** stones.

elim: Commonest, but no genetic clue or ground-glass look.
Radiolucent; not the familial ground-glass stone.

steps.x: **B. Cystine.** Familial + ground-glass = cystine; treat with penicillamine.

practice.stem: A 44 year old woman with a known 8 mm left ureteric stone has new rigors and constant left loin pain. Her temperature is 39.1°C, pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 92/58 mmHg and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute. Ultrasound shows marked left hydronephrosis.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Fever, sepsis and hydronephrosis behind a ureteric stone mean an infected obstructed kidney. Emphysematous pyelonephritis needs gas in the kidney, usually in diabetics.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a complication in a known stone patient.
Stone + hydronephrosis + fever + shock.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: An **infected obstructed kidney**, needing urgent decompression.

elim: Gas in the kidney in diabetics; not stated.
Follows trauma or anticoagulation; no fever.

steps.x: **B. Infected obstructed kidney.** Stone + fever + hydronephrosis = infected obstructed kidney.

practice.stem: A 47 year old man has had two episodes of renal colic. He takes high-dose vitamin C supplements and drinks little water. A plain X-ray shows a small radiopaque stone with smooth surfaces in the left kidney. His urine pH is 6.2.
practice.q: Which is the most likely composition of the stone?
practice.e: Calcium oxalate stones are the most common, radiopaque and smooth, and linked to high-dose vitamin C. Uric acid stones are radiolucent.

steps.x: Stone composition: radiopacity plus diet.
Radiopaque, smooth, vitamin C and dehydration.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Calcium oxalate**, the commonest stone.

elim: Radiolucent and forms in acidic urine below pH 5.5.

steps.x: **A. Calcium oxalate.** Commonest stone, linked to vitamin C = calcium oxalate.

practice.stem: A 31 year old woman who is 24 weeks pregnant has severe intermittent right loin pain radiating to the groin. Her temperature is 37.0°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. Urine dipstick shows blood 2+ and no nitrites.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate imaging investigation?
practice.e: Ultrasound replaces CT KUB in pregnancy to avoid radiation. CT KUB remains the gold standard in non-pregnant adults.

steps.x: Imaging in a special group: pregnancy.
Renal colic in pregnancy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Ultrasound** instead of CT.

elim: Gold standard, but avoided in pregnancy.
No signs of infection, and it is not imaging.

steps.x: **D. Renal ultrasound.** Renal colic in pregnancy = ultrasound.

practice.stem: A 26 year old woman has sudden severe right loin pain radiating to the groin. Her last period was 6 weeks ago. Her pulse rate is 106 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg. Urine dipstick shows blood 1+ and no nitrites or leucocytes.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
practice.e: In women of childbearing age with suspected renal colic, a pregnancy test excludes ectopic pregnancy and decides the imaging. CT comes after.

steps.x: 'Next' investigation in a woman of childbearing age.
Possible renal colic, but she may be pregnant.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Pregnancy test** first: exclude ectopic and decide on CT vs ultrasound.

elim: Do not scan before excluding pregnancy.

steps.x: **E. Urine pregnancy test.** Woman of childbearing age with loin pain = pregnancy test.

practice.stem: A 37 year old man has severe left renal colic. His temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 144/90 mmHg. He has no allergies, normal renal function and no history of peptic ulcer or asthma.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial analgesia?
practice.e: NSAIDs such as IM diclofenac are first-line for renal colic. IV paracetamol is used if NSAIDs are contraindicated or insufficient.

steps.x: Initial analgesia: the first-line drug class.

clues: no history of peptic ulcer or asthma
steps.x: No contraindication to NSAIDs.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **NSAID**: one-off IM diclofenac.

elim: Opioids are not first-line for renal colic.
IV paracetamol is the alternative only if NSAIDs fail or are contraindicated.

steps.x: **A. Intramuscular diclofenac.** Renal colic analgesia = NSAID first (IM diclofenac).

practice.stem: A 40 year old man has renal colic. CT KUB shows a 6 mm stone in the distal left ureter with no hydronephrosis. His pain is controlled with diclofenac. He is apyrexial and his creatinine is normal.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Stones under 10 mm can be helped to pass with tamsulosin. Watchful waiting alone is for asymptomatic stones under 5 mm.

steps.x: Management by stone size.
Symptomatic stone under 10 mm, no infection or obstruction.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Tamsulosin** for medical expulsive therapy.

elim: Prevents recurrence; does not help this stone pass.
For stones over 2 cm or staghorn.
Only for asymptomatic stones under 5 mm.

steps.x: **D. Tamsulosin.** <10 mm = tamsulosin.

practice.stem: A 50 year old woman has a 9 mm right ureteric stone with hydronephrosis. She now has a temperature of 38.8°C, pulse rate 118 bpm and BP 94/60 mmHg. Her creatinine has risen from 80 to 190 µmol/L.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: An infected obstructed kidney with AKI needs urgent percutaneous nephrostomy plus IV antibiotics. Antibiotics alone cannot clear an obstructed system.

steps.x: Emergency management.
Infected obstructed kidney with AKI.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Decompress: **percutaneous nephrostomy** plus IV antibiotics.

elim: Never in active infection with obstruction.
Cannot clear pus behind the blockage.

steps.x: **E. Urgent nephrostomy and IV antibiotics.** Infected + obstructed = drain it now.

practice.stem: A 61 year old woman has recurrent Proteus mirabilis urinary tract infections. Imaging shows a staghorn calculus. Her urine pH is 8.2. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of stone formation?
o: Acidic urine from high purine turnover
practice.e: Proteus urease splits urea into ammonia, raising urine pH and precipitating magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite). Acidic urine favours uric acid.

steps.x: Mechanism of the stone in the vignette.
Proteus, staghorn, alkaline urine: struvite.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Urease** splits urea to ammonia, raising pH; magnesium ammonium phosphate precipitates.
**E. Urease splitting urea into ammonia.** Struvite = urease = alkaline urine.
